## Life Summary

Vida was the only child of [[James Telfer (1866–1946)]] and his wife [[Alma Sporer (1881–1965)]], born on 8 March 1919 at Glencoe West, South Australia. She was active in the Glencoe community from a young age, participating in local school concerts and church events with the Templer family.

She was remembered as a loving mother to Peter and Julie, grandmother to Paul and Debbie, and great-grandmother to Kate, Zara, Angus, and Ellie. She was also a foster mother to Laura (deceased).

# Wilhelm Seebohm

**Born:** 26 Sep 1833, Altona (near Hamburg), Germany | **Died:** 26 Dec 1907, Tantanoola, South Australia | **Buried:** Tantanoola Cemetery

German immigrant, father of Julia Matilda Seebohm and ten other children. Emigrated from Altona, near Hamburg, Germany, arriving in Australia around 1850. Naturalised South Australian farmer, poundkeeper, and prominent Tantanoola community member.

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|---|---|
| **Spouse** | [[Mary Anne McIntyre (1836–1913)]] |
| **Daughter** | [[Julia Matilda Seebohm (1876–1939)]] |
| **Children** | William Alexander, Elizabeth, Duncan Edward, Mary Agatha, Augusta John, Annabella, Peter Colin, Janet, Edward Dugal, Murdoch Alexander |

## Life Summary

Wilhelm Seebohm was born on 26 September 1833 in Altona, near Hamburg, Germany. He emigrated from Germany, arriving in Australia around 1850–1853, and settled in the Mount Gambier / Tantanoola district of South Australia's South East region.

He married Scottish-born Mary Anne McIntyre, a fellow immigrant from Glasgow who had arrived in Australia on the ship *New Zealander* in 1852. They settled on O.B. Flat as their first home, then moved through Glencoe, Tarpeena, Rivoli Bay, and Reedy Creek before finally settling on Tantanoola Creek, where they successfully established a dairy farm and built a family home.

Wilhelm served as the local **poundkeeper** for many years and was the first member initiated at the inauguration of the local **Oddfellows' Lodge**. He also held the position of honorary secretary of the local A. and F. (Agricultural and Friendly) Society and was an active member of the Presbyterian church, serving as **Superintendent of the Presbyterian Sunday-school** for some time.

Known as a man of "kindly and retiring disposition," he was "liked by all who knew him." He and Mary raised a family of **six sons and five daughters** at Tantanoola.

Wilhelm died on Boxing Day (26 December) 1907 at Tantanoola, aged 74. His funeral at Tantanoola Cemetery was attended by 32 vehicles in cortege, with Rev. G. Martin officiating. His obituary in *The Border Watch* noted he was the first member of the local Oddfellows' Lodge and a respected community figure.

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 26 Sep 1833 | Born in Altona, Hamburg, Germany |
| c.1850–1853 | Emigrated to Australia (came via Hull, England on the ship *Helen Mac Gregor*, 25 Apr 1853) |
| c.1857–1858 | Married Mary Anne McIntyre at Casterton, Victoria |
| c.1867–1868 | Settled in the Tantanoola district |
| 26 Dec 1907 | Died at Tantanoola, South Australia |
| ~28 Dec 1907 | Buried at Tantanoola Cemetery |

## Newspaper References

> **Obituary — The Border Watch, 4 January 1908**
> The death occurred on Boxing morning, of Mr. William Seebohm, at the age of 74 years. The deceased was a native of Hamburg, Germany, and came to Australia in 1850. He settled in the district about 40 years ago. He was the first member initiated at the inauguration of the local Oddfellows' Lodge, held the position of poundkeeper for a number of years, and was sometime hon. secretary of the A. and F. Society. He was also active in church matters, especially those of the Presbyterian church, and was for some time superintendent of the Presbyterian Sunday-school. A man of kindly and retiring disposition, he was liked by all who knew him. He leaves a widow and a grown-up family of six sons and five daughters. The funeral took place at the Tantanoola Cemetery on Friday afternoon, the cortege numbering 32 vehicles. Rev. G. Martin officiated.

**Source:** [Trove: The Border Watch, 4 Jan 1908, p.3](https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/77443538) — accessed 14 June 2026

![[Family History/People/Photos/william-seebohm-grave.jpg|400]]
> Grave of Wilhelm Seebohm at Tantanoola Cemetery
**Source:** [FindAGrave: William Seebohm (memorial 186971060)](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/186971060/william-seebohm) — accessed 14 June 2026

## Notes

- Known as "Wilhelm" or "William" in family records
- The Seebohm family were German immigrants who settled at Tantanoola in the same era and area as the Telfer family, which explains how Julia met Mark Telfer
- Listed as father of Julia Matilda Seebohm in WikiTree (Seebohm-10) and Augusta John Seebohm's obituary

The funeral took place at the Tantanoola Cemetery on Friday afternoon, the cortege numbering 32 vehicles. Rev. G. Martin officiated.

# William John Baker (1831–1919)

## Summary

| Detail | Info |
|---|---|
| **Full Name** | William John Baker |
| **Born** | 14 Apr 1831 — Bickleigh, Devon, England |
| **Died** | 3 Jun 1919 (age 88) — Hyde Park, South Australia |
| **Buried** | West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide, SA |
| **Spouse** | [[Sophia Baker (1829–1901)|Sophia Marsh]] (m. 9 Mar 1853, Adelaide) |
| **Occupation** | Mason, Farmer |
| **Parents** | James Baker & Jane Baker (of Bickleigh, Devonshire) |

---

## Early Life

William John Baker was born on **14 Apr 1831** in Bickleigh, Devonshire, England, the son of **James Baker** and **Jane Baker**. His early years were spent in the Devonshire countryside.

At age **19**, he emigrated to South Australia aboard the **Stag** (678 tons, Captain John Baker), departing **Plymouth on 22 Feb 1850** and arriving **Port Adelaide on 11 June 1850**. The passenger list records him as "William Baker, 19, Mason, Devon" — confirming both his age (born ~1831, supporting the 1831 date over 1829) and his trade as a **mason** (stone worker/builder), not a baker.

---

## Life in South Australia

Upon arrival, his first job was helping build a church in Adelaide. When work stalled, he and a friend walked through the countryside seeking work, sleeping in barns and empty houses. He later joined the **first gold rushes to Victoria**.

He married **[[Sophia Baker (1829–1901)|Sophia Marsh]]** on **9 March 1853** in Adelaide, South Australia. Sophia had arrived in the colony on 31 July 1846 with her parents **[[Joseph March (1797–1883)]]** and **Sophia Webster** aboard the ship *Canton*.

William and Sophia took up land near **Virginia** on the Adelaide Plains, farming and working as a mason. To earn income while clearing land, he used a team of bullocks to cart goods to the Burra copper mines and return with copper ore. He purchased Sections 4102, 4095, and 4096 near Stebonheath Davoren Road.

They settled in the **Gawler Plains / Peachy Belt / Port Gawler** area and raised **nine children** — five sons and four daughters.

---

|---|---|---|---|
| William Baker | 17 Dec 1853, Gawler Plains | — | Father of 8 |
| **[[Hannah Parker (1855–1948)|Hannah Baker]]** | **28 Aug 1855, Peachy Belt** | **1948** | **Married [[William Humphrey Parker (1850–1926)]] — your direct line** |
| Emeline (Couzens) | 29 Sep 1857, Port Adelaide | — | Mother of 5 |

| Alfred Baker | 1 Aug 1861, Peachy Belt | — | Father of 5 |

| Sophia Harriett (Ridgway) | 10 Aug 1868, Port Gawler | — | Mother of 4 |
| Phineas Baker | 11 Nov 1870, Virginia | — | Father of 7 |

---

## Later Life & Death

William died on **3 June 1919** in Hyde Park, a suburb of Adelaide, at approximately age 88. He is buried at **West Terrace Cemetery**, Adelaide. His wife Sophia predeceased him, dying on 1 Dec 1901 aged 72. Both are in the same grave at West Terrace Cemetery.

---

- **WikiTree:** [Baker-1805](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Baker-1805) — confirms birth 14 Apr 1831, Bickleigh Devon; parents James Baker & Jane Baker
- **Marriage:** William John Baker to Sophia Marsh, 9 Mar 1853, Adelaide, SA (Genealogy SA, Book 15, Page 73)
- **Passenger list — *Stag* 1850:** [Bound for South Australia — 1850Stag](https://bound-for-south-australia.collections.slsa.gov.au/1850Stag.htm) — confirms "William Baker, 19, Mason, Devon"
- **SA Maritime Museum:** [Passengers in History — node/572452](https://passengers.history.sa.gov.au/node/572452)

- **Burial:** West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide, SA

---

## Research Notes

- **Birth year 1829 vs 1831:** The vault previously recorded 1829. The *Stag* passenger list (age 19 arriving June 1850) confirms ~1831 birth. WikiTree and Playford's Past both say 14 Apr 1831. Changed to 1831.
- **Parents:** Three secondary sources (Playford's Past, WikiTree, ianfoster.com.au) all state **James and Jane Baker** of Bickleigh, Devonshire. No primary source (baptism record or death certificate transcription) has been located yet — this remains the top priority for verification.
- **Sophia's surname:** Playford's Past records her as "Sophia Marsh" (not "March"). The vault uses "March" — to be investigated further.
- **Next step:** Request SA death registration transcript from Genealogy SA (~AUD $27.50) for primary source proof of parents' names.

William John Baker was born on **14 Apr 1831** in Bickleigh, Devonshire, England, the son of **James Baker** and **Jane Baker**. His early years were spent in the Devonshire countryside.

At age **19**, he emigrated to South Australia aboard the **Stag** (678 tons, Captain John Baker), departing **Plymouth on 22 Feb 1850** and arriving **Port Adelaide on 11 June 1850**. The passenger list records him as "William Baker, 19, Mason, Devon" — confirming both his age (born ~1831, supporting the 1831 date over 1829) and his trade as a **mason** (stone worker/builder), not a baker.

---

## Life in South Australia

Upon arrival, his first job was helping build a church in Adelaide. When work stalled, he and a friend walked through the countryside seeking work, sleeping in barns and empty houses. He later joined the **first gold rushes to Victoria**.

He married **[[Sophia Baker (1829–1901)|Sophia Marsh]]** on **9 March 1853** in Adelaide, South Australia. Sophia had arrived in the colony on 31 July 1846 with her parents **[[Joseph March (1797–1883)]]** and **Sophia Webster** aboard the ship *Canton*.

William and Sophia took up land near **Virginia** on the Adelaide Plains, farming and working as a mason. To earn income while clearing land, he used a team of bullocks to cart goods to the Burra copper mines and return with copper ore. He purchased Sections 4102, 4095, and 4096 near Stebonheath Davoren Road.

They settled in the **Gawler Plains / Peachy Belt / Port Gawler** area and raised **nine children** — five sons and four daughters.

---

| Sophia Harriett (Ridgway) | 10 Aug 1868, Port Gawler | — | Mother of 4 |
| Phineas Baker | 11 Nov 1870, Virginia | — | Father of 7 |

---

## Later Life & Death

William died on **3 June 1919** in Hyde Park, a suburb of Adelaide, at approximately age 88. He is buried at **West Terrace Cemetery**, Adelaide. His wife Sophia predeceased him, dying on 1 Dec 1901 aged 72. Both are in the same grave at West Terrace Cemetery.

## Sources

- **WikiTree:** [Baker-1805](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Baker-1805) — confirms birth 14 Apr 1831, Bickleigh Devon; parents James Baker & Jane Baker
- **Marriage:** William John Baker to Sophia Marsh, 9 Mar 1853, Adelaide, SA (Genealogy SA, Book 15, Page 73)
- **Passenger list — *Stag* 1850:** [Bound for South Australia — 1850Stag](https://bound-for-south-australia.collections.slsa.gov.au/1850Stag.htm) — confirms "William Baker, 19, Mason, Devon"

## Research Notes

- **Birth year 1829 vs 1831:** The vault previously recorded 1829. The *Stag* passenger list (age 19 arriving June 1850) confirms ~1831 birth. WikiTree and Playford's Past both say 14 Apr 1831. Changed to 1831.
- **Parents:** Three secondary sources (Playford's Past, WikiTree, ianfoster.com.au) all state **James and Jane Baker** of Bickleigh, Devonshire. No primary source (baptism record or death certificate transcription) has been located yet — this remains the top priority for verification.
- **Sophia's surname:** Playford's Past records her as "Sophia Marsh" (not "March"). The vault uses "March" — to be investigated further.
